title: Words in Context
summary: Predict the meaning before you look at the choices.

blocks.html: The move
Read the sentence, cover the four choices, and predict a simple word that fits. Then pick the choice closest to your prediction.
Check three things: meaning, tone, and logic. A word can be advanced and still be wrong.
Example: “Although the results were disappointing, the team remained ___.” The contrast word “although” tells you the team stayed hopeful or persistent, not discouraged.
Common traps

• A word that sounds academic but does not fit the sentence.
  • A word with the right meaning but the wrong tone.
  • A word that fits the first half of the sentence but breaks the logic of the second half.

title: Text Structure & Purpose
summary: Ask what each sentence is doing, not just what it says.

blocks.html: The move
Label each sentence with a job: claim, evidence, example, contrast, problem, or solution. Then match the question to the job.
Common structures are problem–solution, misconception–correction, claim–evidence, and comparison.
If the first sentence says what people usually believe and the next says “In fact,” the passage is probably correcting a misconception.
Common traps

• A true statement that does not describe the structure.
  • A choice that describes one detail instead of the whole passage.
  • A choice that uses the right words but reverses the relationship.

title: Cross-Text Connections
summary: Summarize each text in one sentence, then compare.

blocks.html: The move
Write a one-sentence summary of Text 1 and Text 2. Then ask: do they agree, disagree, qualify each other, or discuss different aspects of the same issue?
Look for response words such as “however,” “yet,” “although,” and “in addition.”
Do not assume the authors disagree just because they focus on different details. One may be adding a complication to the other's point.
Common traps

• Choosing a relationship that is stronger than the texts support.
  • Confusing “different emphasis” with “opposite opinion.”
  • Ignoring a qualifier such as “in some cases.”

title: Central Ideas & Details
summary: Main idea first, exact detail second.

blocks.html: The move
For main-idea questions, ask what the passage is mostly about. The answer should cover the whole passage, not one interesting detail.
For detail questions, go back to the text and find the exact sentence. Do not rely on memory.
A correct main idea is broad enough to cover the passage but narrow enough to be meaningful. “Birds are interesting” is too broad; “A tracking study revealed a new migration route” is specific.
Common traps

• A true detail that is too narrow to be the main idea.
  • A statement that is broader than the passage.
  • An answer that adds information the passage never states.

title: Command of Evidence — Textual
summary: The evidence must directly support the claim.

blocks.html: The move
Find the claim first. Then test each choice by asking: if this were true, would the claim become more believable?
The best evidence is specific, relevant, and directly connected to the claim.
A statement can be true and still be wrong if it does not support the specific claim.
Common traps

• Evidence that supports a different claim.
  • Evidence that is too general.
  • A quotation that mentions the topic but not the claim.

title: Command of Evidence — Quantitative
summary: Read the labels, units, and exact comparison.

blocks.html: The move
Read the graph or table title, axis labels, and units before you look at the choices. Then match the exact trend, value, or comparison in the claim.
Check whether the claim is about an increase, a decrease, a difference, or a highest/lowest value.
A choice can contain a correct number and still be wrong if it answers the wrong question.
Common traps

• Mixing up percentages and raw numbers.
  • Ignoring the units.
  • Choosing a true fact that does not support the claim.

title: Inferences
summary: Make the smallest logical step, not a leap.

blocks.html: The move
Treat an inference like a “must be true” question. The answer has to follow from the text, even if it is not stated word for word.
Ask: what would a careful reader conclude from these details?
If the passage says the road was closed after a storm and drivers took a longer route, you can infer the storm affected the road. You cannot infer the exact amount of damage.
Common traps

• A reasonable idea that the passage never supports.
  • An overstatement of what the passage says.
  • A prediction about the future that is not justified.

title: Rhetorical Synthesis
summary: Read the goal first, then use only the notes.

blocks.html: The move
Read the goal before the bullet notes. Then choose the sentence that accomplishes that goal using the relevant notes.
Do not add outside information. Do not include an interesting note that does not help the goal.
If the goal is to emphasize a contrast, the best sentence will put the two contrasting facts next to each other.
Common traps

• A sentence that is accurate but does not meet the goal.
  • A sentence that includes irrelevant notes.
  • A sentence that changes the meaning of a note.

title: Transitions
summary: Name the relationship before you choose the word.

blocks.html: The move
Cover the choices and describe the relationship between the two sentences: contrast, cause and effect, addition, example, or sequence.
Then choose the transition that signals that exact relationship.
Contrast: however, nevertheless, although. Cause/effect: therefore, consequently, as a result. Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition.
Common traps

• A transition that sounds sophisticated but signals the wrong relationship.
  • Choosing a cause/effect word when the sentences are actually contrasting.
  • Ignoring a “not” or “never” that flips the logic.

title: Boundaries
summary: Decide whether the parts are complete sentences, lists, or extra information.

blocks.html: The move
Check whether each side of the blank can stand alone as a complete sentence.
Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, or a comma + coordinating conjunction. A colon introduces a list or explanation. A dash can add emphasis.
A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences. That is a comma splice.
Common traps

• Using a comma between two independent clauses.
  • Using a semicolon before a list instead of a colon.
  • Adding punctuation that turns a complete sentence into a fragment.

title: Form, Structure, and Sense
summary: Find the real subject and match the verb.

blocks.html: The move
For subject–verb agreement, find the subject and ignore prepositional phrases. “The number of students” is singular because the subject is “number.”
Check pronoun agreement, verb tense, modifiers, and parallelism the same way: find the word being described or matched.
A verb agrees with its subject, not with the nearest noun. “Neither the teacher nor the students were ready” uses “were” because the closer subject is plural.
Common traps

• Matching the verb to the noun immediately before it.
  • Using a singular pronoun for a plural antecedent.
  • Putting a modifier next to the wrong noun.

title: Reading & Writing Pacing
summary: Read for structure, answer with evidence, and keep moving.

blocks.html: The move
Read the question first when it asks about a specific function or evidence. For main-idea questions, read the whole passage quickly and then answer.
For grammar questions, read the sentence without the blank first. Your ear will often catch the error.
Flag a question if it takes too long and come back. Do not let one hard question eat the section.
Time targets

• About 70–75 seconds per Reading & Writing question.
  • Leave 2–3 minutes at the end to check flagged questions.
  • If two answers seem correct, choose the one that is more precise and directly supported.
